analysis.one_liner: Repeals the rule requiring the president to propose Medicare cuts when general revenues cover too much of Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2006, referred to two House committees, sent to a Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote; it died with no cosponsors when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Medicare law included a cost-containment mechanism: if general tax revenues ever cover more than 45% of total Medicare costs for two years running, the president must send Congress a proposal to cut Medicare spending. This bill would wipe out that mechanism entirely, restoring the law as if the provision had never been enacted. It was introduced by Rep. Robert Wexler and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would no longer face a built-in trigger that obligates the president to propose Medicare benefit or payment cuts whenever general tax revenues cover more than 45% of Medicare's costs. Hospitals, doctors, and other providers paid by Medicare would also be spared from the payment-reduction proposals such a trigger could set in motion.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals subtitle A of title VIII of the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 and restores the affected provisions of law as if that subtitle had never been enacted [S3].

By removing the Medicare funding-warning mechanism, the bill would eliminate the legal requirement that the president submit cost-cutting legislation whenever general revenues exceed 45% of Medicare outlays, shielding beneficiaries from automatically proposed cuts.
The CRS summary confirms the bill's sole purpose is to repeal the Medicare cost containment provisions of the 2003 Medicare law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and the general-revenue side of the budget. Repealing the cost-containment trigger removes one of the few statutory mechanisms designed to flag and force action on Medicare's growing call on general tax revenues, so the program's long-term financing gap would face less built-in pressure for correction.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the cost-containment provisions would remove a statutory warning system aimed at Medicare's long-term financing shortfall, leaving no required mechanism for the president and Congress to confront Medicare's rising share of general tax spending [S2][S3].

The practical benefit to beneficiaries is limited: the existing mechanism only requires the president to propose cuts — it does not impose them, and Congress would still have to pass any proposal — so repeal changes little in the short run while eliminating an early-warning tool.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers beneficiaries modest, real protection against a trigger designed to generate Medicare cut proposals, but the cost is real too: it deletes one of the few automatic signals forcing Washington to face Medicare's financing gap. Because the trigger only compels a proposal rather than actual cuts, the bill's practical effect is small in both directions — a low-stakes repeal that leans toward protecting current beneficiaries at the expense of a long-term budget check.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee and then in a Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2007, without a hearing, a markup, or a vote of any kind.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Wexler introduced the bill in the House on May 25, 2006 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce for the portions within their jurisdiction [S5].
On June 5, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill drew zero cosponsors [S4] and never received a vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much: because the trigger only requires a presidential proposal rather than actual cuts, its repeal would have been a modest shield for Medicare beneficiaries, and its death simply leaves the existing warning mechanism on the books. Deficit-focused policymakers who value the cost-containment tool are the only side better off that it never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The funding-warning law stayed on the books

for.name: Rep. Robert Wexler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Medicare cost containment provisions; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 25, 2006 and never took it up; no hearing or markup was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Second referral committee (jurisdiction over Medicare provisions)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 25, 2006 and never scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and it never reached a floor vote, so no partisan voting pattern exists.

industries.industry: Hospitals, physicians, and other Medicare providers
industries.note: Repeal would spare Medicare providers from the payment-reduction proposals the funding-warning trigger is designed to produce, and beneficiaries would benefit alongside them since provider cuts and benefit cuts travel together in Medicare. The direct effect is modest because the trigger only compels proposals, not cuts.
